newsitem.title: USA: McLaren's neighbors urge firm action in Texas siege.
newsitem.headline: McLaren's neighbors urge firm action in Texas siege.

text.p: Driven from their resort homes by a five-day standoff between armed separatists and police in west Texas, local residents are demanding a quick end to the crisis, even if it means bloodshed.

Virtually everyone in this town of 1,200 blames Republic of Texas leader Richard McLaren for the standoff and many are critical of the kid-glove treatment they believe he is getting in negotiations with police surrounding his isolated compound.
"He loves attention and he is getting exactly what he wants," said Sandy Ohlsen, who has been unable to return to her mountain home about 20 miles from here since the start of the siege last Sunday.

Like most of the estimated 120 people who left the Davis Mountains Resort area where the Republic's compound is located, Ohlsen and her husband were staying with friends in the area but worry the standoff could last for weeks.
"If they are only going to negotiate with him, then we could be out of our homes a long time. He could talk for months," she said.

McLaren is holed up with 12 followers and has refused to turn himself in to police to face felony charges of engaging in organised criminal activity. Six of the 13 Republic members, who claim Texas is an independent nation and that they form its provisional government, face this charge.

Three of them are also wanted for aggravated kidnapping after they seized two neighbours, Joe and Margaret Rowe, at gunpoint at the start of the standoff and held them for 12 hours before releasing them in a prisoner exchange deal.

Police made clear they want a negotiated solution and have no plans to force McLaren out. That attitude upset residents, many of them retirees drawn to the area by its spectacular wooded mountains and surrounding high desert plains.

"We want the law to go in there and take him out for good," said Suzanne Parchment, whose son persuaded her to leave her home shortly after the siege began. She said she felt sorry for McLaren when he first moved to the area about a decade ago and helped him get jobs as a handyman but his character changed almost overnight.
"Now he's totally lost it," she said.
Some residents have been even more vocal in calling for firm action. "They should go in and kill that son of a bitch," said Jimmy Gallego, a retiree in the nearby town of Alpine.
But others, while hoping for a quick solution, urged caution. "These weirdos are not worth the bloodshed of even a single officer," Fort Davis store owner Andrew Clark said.
His wife Beverly disagreed. "I think they should go in and kill him. I know that sounds mean but they been pushing people around long enough," she said.

McLaren's problems with his neighbours started years ago when he began filing liens against several of them in a bitter dispute over land rights in the 6,000-acre resort area. They got steadily worse as he became involved in the Republic of Texas, using the same strategy of filing liens against government officials and property owners across Texas.
Local residents say the situation became unbearable when other Republic of Texas members joined McLaren at his compound and allegedly began intimidating neighbours with guns.
"Everybody hates them. It's just a bunch of macho men beating their chests and they are just hurting this town," said Rosalinda Ramirez-Gonzalez, a local dog trainer.
